bib.title: Natural Language Processing (almost) from Scratch
bib.venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research (arXiv:1103.0398v1 copy)

read.skipped: Last gradient derivations of Appendix A (sentence-level log-likelihood accumulation) and the reference list were skimmed only.

question: Can one unified neural network, with word embeddings learned from large unlabeled text, match task-engineered systems on POS, chunking, NER and semantic role labeling?
hypothesis: Intermediate representations (word embeddings) learned from vast unlabeled data are more general than any single benchmark and can replace task-specific engineered features.
contributions: A unified window/convolutional neural architecture with a word lookup table, trained end-to-end for four tagging tasks
Sentence-level log-likelihood (CRF-like transition scores) for tagging
Word embeddings from a pairwise ranking language model trained on Wikipedia and Reuters, used to initialise supervised networks
Multitask training study and a study of added task-specific engineering
SENNA, a fast, small-memory C tagger

method.summary: Words are mapped by a trainable lookup table to dense vectors (50-d plus a 5-d capitalisation feature), fed to a window network (POS, CHUNK, NER) or a convolution plus max-over-time sentence network (SRL), and trained with word-level or sentence-level log-likelihood. The lookup table is optionally initialised from embeddings learned by a window-based language model trained with a pairwise ranking loss on 631M (LM1) then 852M (LM2) words of unlabeled text.
method.task: Sequence tagging (POS, chunking, NER, SRL) with unsupervised word-embedding pretraining

models.name: Window approach NN

training.objective: Supervised: word-level (softmax) or sentence-level log-likelihood (path score = transition + network scores, Viterbi decoding). Language model: pairwise ranking sum over x and replacement words w of max(0, 1 - f(x) + f(x(w))), where x(w) replaces the centre word.
training.optimizer: stochastic gradient (one example at a time)
training.lr: 0.01 supervised (Table 5); divided by layer fan-in, kept fixed
training.batch_size: inferred: 1 (one random example per step, Eq. 17; LM samples one sentence-word pair per iteration)
training.tokens: LM1 trained on 631M words, LM2 additionally on 852M-word corpus
training.wall_clock: LM1 about four weeks; LM2 an additional three weeks; supervised: CHUNK and NER about one hour, POS a few hours, SRL about three days
training.seeds: 5 runs for Fig 4 std; 10 runs for the ensemble study; fixed initial parameters per task otherwise

other.init: uniform, variance tied to inverse square root of fan-in (fan-in 1 for lookup table)
other.model_selection: breeding: k parallel runs, best by ranking criterion on 1M-word Wikipedia validation chosen and perturbed; hyperparameters searched: learning rate, embedding dim, hidden units, window size
other.multitask: alternate examples across tasks, equal weight, shared lookup tables and first layer

inference.decoding: Viterbi over tag paths for sentence-level likelihood; argmax per word for word-level
inference.samples: single model; ensemble experiment uses 10 runs with different initialisation

limits: Authors concede that lowercasing and the caps feature mean it is only 'almost' from scratch; characters-only input is called beyond scope.
Full hyperparameter grid search was infeasible; LM hyperparameters chosen by 'breeding' and arbitrary dictionary schedule, and the LM learning rate is not stated.
Language model is window-based and unidirectional context only in the sense of a fixed window, which authors call probably too restrictive; only embeddings are transferred.
SRL still trails the benchmark (75.49 vs 77.92) without parse trees; the benchmark uses six parse trees.
Word embeddings are one vector per word type; no sub-word handling, so rare words map to RARE (100,000 word dictionary).
Dated: fixed-window feed-forward models, HardTanh, per-example SGD and CoNLL-era benchmarks pre-date recurrent and transformer models.

terms.definition: LTW(w) = column w of a trainable matrix W of size d_wrd x |D|, mapping a word index to a feature vector trained by backpropagation
Tag-path score is the sum of transition scores and network scores, normalised over all tag paths (CRF-like, without per-step normalisation)
